payload.name: bronchiole
payload.scope: People made the bronchiole construct to map the cartilage-free segment of the bronchial tree distal to the segmental bronchi, so that pathologists can identify the conducting-respiratory boundary and pulmonologists can categorize small-airways disease.

definition.body: The bronchiole is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps the cartilage-free airway branches of the bronchial tree distal to the segmental bronchi. Parameters: (1) the wall architecture — lacking hyaline cartilage plates and submucosal glands, with a wall composed of smooth muscle, elastic fibers, and a mucosal lining; (2) the epithelial lining — transitioning from pseudostratified ciliated columnar with goblet cells proximally to simple cuboidal with Club and ciliated cells distally; (3) the diameter — generally under 1 mm internal caliber, distinguishing it from the cartilage-bearing bronchi; (4) the functional classification — divided into terminal bronchioles (purely conducting) and respiratory bronchioles (transitional, with scattered gas-exchange alveoli in the wall). It persists as a maintained anatomical landmark in pulmonary histology, respiratory physiology, and clinical small-airways assessment. e.g.: the bronchiole described in Junqueira Basic Histology, 15th edition; airway resistance contribution of bronchioles per West Respiratory Physiology, 10th edition; bronchiolar smooth muscle reactivity in asthma per GINA guidelines | not: the bronchus; the alveolus [formal: bronchiolus pulmonis | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.name: terminal-bronchiole
payload.scope: People made the terminal-bronchiole construct to map the last purely conducting airway of the tree, so that pathologists mark the conducting-respiratory transition and pulmonologists localize where small-airways disease begins.

definition.body: The terminal bronchiole is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps the most distal airway of the purely conducting portion of the bronchial tree, the airway immediately proximal to the respiratory bronchiole. Parameters: (1) the position in the conducting path — the final rung of the accepted airway hierarchy, the path running subsegmental bronchus, terminal bronchiole, respiratory bronchiole, alveolar duct, alveolar sac, alveolus, so the terminal bronchiole is the last airway before the respiratory zone begins; (2) the wall architecture — a smooth-muscle and elastic-fiber sleeve without hyaline cartilage plates and without submucosal glands, its wall perforated by no alveolar openings, which is the map's boundary: the first wall to carry scattered alveolar outpouchings is already the respiratory bronchiole; (3) the epithelial lining — simple cuboidal epithelium with ciliated and Club cells at this distal limit, the last fully ciliated airway; (4) the caliber — under 1 mm internal diameter, below the subsegmental level whose cartilage plates mark the bronchial side of the transition; (5) the functional role — the last airway contributing to conducting-zone airway resistance, so its smooth-muscle tone sets the threshold below which obstruction is a small-airways disease rather than a bronchial one. It persists as a maintained level of the named airway hierarchy in pulmonary histology, respiratory physiology, and small-airways assessment. e.g.: the terminal bronchiole section showing the bronchiolar transition in Junqueira Basic Histology 15th edition; the terminal bronchiole rung in the acinus diagram of West Respiratory Physiology 10th edition; small-airways resistance attributed to terminal bronchioles per GINA bronchial smooth-muscle assessment | not: the respiratory bronchiole (the transitional airway with scattered alveolar outpouchings on its wall); the subsegmental bronchus (the last cartilage-bearing airway proximal to this level); the alveolus (the gas-exchange sac distal to the respiratory zone) [formal: bronchiolus terminalis | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

definition.body: The bronchiole is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps the human-made category of cartilage-free airway branches distal to the segmental bronchi. Parameters: (1) the maker — pulmonary histology and respiratory physiology keep the category, taught since the early 20th century and codified in histology atlases and physiology texts; (2) the boundary — it includes terminal bronchioles and respiratory bronchioles, excludes bronchi with hyaline cartilage plates and submucosal glands, and is distinguished from alveolar ducts and alveolar sacs by the presence or absence of alveolar outpouchings in the wall; (3) the persistence mechanism — the category persists through named diagrams, atlases, teaching slides and clinical small-airways assessment protocols that reference the bronchiole level as the conducting-respiratory transition. It persists as a maintained level in anatomical teaching and clinical small-airways assessment. e.g.: the bronchiole level in Junqueira Basic Histology 15th edition; the bronchiole category in West Respiratory Physiology 10th edition; bronchiolar small-airways resistance in GINA asthma guidelines | not: the bronchus (cartilage-bearing airway proximal to the bronchiole); the alveolus (gas-exchange sac distal to the respiratory bronchiole) [formal: bronchiolus pulmonis | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.name: segmental-bronchus
payload.scope: People made the segmental-bronchus construct to map each airway branch that enters a specific bronchopulmonary segment of a lung, so that surgeons can perform segmental resections and radiologists can localize segmental consolidations.

definition.body: The segmental bronchus is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps the airway branches arising from each lobar bronchus that supply individual bronchopulmonary segments. Parameters: (1) the generation — arising at approximately the 4th to 6th generation from the carina, branching from each lobar bronchus; (2) the segmental supply — each segmental bronchus terminates at a single bronchopulmonary segment, the right lung has 10 segmental bronchi matching its 10 segments, the left lung has 8 to 10; (3) the cartilaginous support — hyaline cartilage plates in the wall, similar in pattern to the main bronchi but smaller in number and size; (4) the bronchoscopic target — each segmental ostium is directly visible by flexible bronchoscopy from the lobar bronchus, serving as the landmark for segmental lavage and biopsy. It persists as a maintained level of the named airway hierarchy in pulmonology, thoracic surgery, and bronchoscopy. e.g.: the segmental bronchus as described in Gray s Anatomy, 42nd edition; bronchoscopic access to the right superior segmental bronchus during bronchial lavage; segmentectomy for primary lung cancer per NCCN guidelines | not: the lobar bronchus (the larger airway proximal to segmental branches); the subsegmental bronchus (the distal branch beyond segmental level, transitioning to cartilage-free airways) [formal: bronchus segmentalis | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.name: main-bronchus
payload.scope: People made the main-bronchus construct to map the two primary airway trunks branching from the tracheal carina into each lung, so that surgeons can access the right and left lungs separately during thoracic procedures.

definition.body: The main bronchus is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps the two primary airway trunks — right and left — that branch from the tracheal carina and enter each lung through the pulmonary hilum. Parameters: (1) the division — the right main bronchus is shorter, wider, and more vertical (approximately 25 degrees from midline), the left main bronchus is longer, narrower, and more horizontal (approximately 45 to 60 degrees); (2) the origin — both arise at the carina at the T4 to T5 vertebral level in adults; (3) the cartilaginous support — C-shaped or irregular hyaline cartilage plates in the wall providing structural patency; (4) the mucosal lining — pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium with goblet cells, continuous with the tracheal lining; (5) the distal branching — the right main bronchus gives rise to the superior, middle, and inferior lobar bronchi, the left main bronchus to the superior and inferior lobar bronchi. It persists as a maintained landmark in pulmonology, thoracic surgery, and radiology. e.g.: the main bronchus as described in Gray s Anatomy, 42nd edition; right main bronchus intubation during emergency bronchoscopy; chest CT showing the carina and main bronchial bifurcation | not: the trachea (the single airway proximal to the main bronchi); the lobar bronchus (the distal branch arising from each main bronchus) [formal: bronchus principalis | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.name: terminal-bronchiole
payload.scope: People made the terminal-bronchiole construct to map the most distal purely conducting airway, so that histologists can identify the boundary between conducting and respiratory zones and clinicians can assess small-airways disease.

definition.body: The terminal bronchiole is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps the most distal purely conducting airway in the respiratory tree, terminating at the transition to the respiratory zone. Parameters: (1) the position in the hierarchy - branching from each subsegmental bronchus and giving rise to one or two respiratory bronchioles, approximately the 15th to 16th generation from the trachea; (2) the wall architecture - a thin-walled tube without cartilage or submucosal glands, lined by simple cuboidal epithelium with ciliated cells and Clara (club) cells that secrete surfactant-like material and detoxify inhaled substances; (3) the smooth-muscle component - a relatively thick circumferential smooth muscle layer that can significantly narrow the lumen, making terminal bronchioles the primary site of airway resistance in the conducting zone; (4) the functional boundary - the last airway generation with no alveolar outpouchings in its wall, immediately proximal to the respiratory bronchiole where gas exchange begins. It persists as a maintained landmark in pulmonary histology, respiratory physiology, and occupational lung disease assessment. e.g.: the terminal bronchiole as described in Junqueira Basic Histology, 15th edition; small-airways disease assessment by methacholine challenge testing per ATS guidelines; the terminal bronchiole as the site of centrilobular emphysema in West Respiratory Physiology, 10th edition | not: the respiratory bronchiole (the transitional airway where alveolar outpouchings first appear in the wall); the subsegmental bronchus (the proximal cartilage-bearing airway, a generation more central) [formal: bronchiolus terminalis | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

It persists as a maintained landmark in pulmonary histology, respiratory physiology, and occupational lung disease assessment. e.g.: the terminal bronchiole as described in Junqueira Basic Histology, 15th edition; small-airways disease assessment by methacholine challenge testing per ATS guidelines; the terminal bronchiole as the site of centrilobular emphysema in West Respiratory Physiology, 10th edition | not: the respiratory bronchiole (the transitional airway where alveolar outpouchings first appear in the wall); the subsegmental bronchus (the proximal cartilage-bearing airway, a generation more central) [formal: bronchiolus terminalis | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.name: bronchial-tree
payload.scope: People made the bronchial-tree construct to map the hierarchical branching pattern of conducting airways from the tracheal bifurcation to the terminal respiratory units, so that clinicians can navigate the bronchial tree during bronchoscopy and surgeons can plan resections by segment.

definition.body: The bronchial tree is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps the hierarchical branching pattern of the conducting airways from the tracheal bifurcation to the terminal respiratory units. Parameters: (1) the hierarchy — main bronchi dividing into lobar bronchi, then segmental, subsegmental, and finally cartilage-free bronchioles and respiratory bronchioles, each generation branching into progressively smaller airways; (2) the lobar organization — the right tree has three lobar branches (superior, middle, inferior) and the left has two (superior, inferior), reflecting the asymmetry of the lungs; (3) the segmental organization — each lobar bronchus supplies named bronchopulmonary segments, each with its own segmental and subsegmental airway; (4) the functional gradient — cartilage decreases and smooth muscle increases distally, with the transition from conducting to gas-exchange airways at the respiratory bronchiole level. It persists as a maintained structural framework in pulmonary histology, respiratory physiology, bronchoscopic navigation, and thoracic surgery. e.g.: the bronchial tree classification in Gray's Anatomy 42nd edition; bronchographic visualization of the right bronchial tree in radiographic anatomy texts; the bronchial tree hierarchy used for bronchoscopic segment identification in clinical pulmonology | not: the trachea (the single proximal airway feeding the tree); the lung (the organ containing the bronchial tree, broader anatomical structure) [formal: arbor bronchialis | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.name: pulmonary-acinus
payload.scope: People made the pulmonary-acinus construct to map the functional gas-exchange unit of the lung distal to a terminal bronchiole, so that physiologists can quantify surface area, pathologists can grade emphysema, and clinicians can understand regional ventilation patterns.

definition.body: The pulmonary acinus is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps the functional gas-exchange unit of the lung, comprising the respiratory bronchiole, alveolar ducts, and alveolar sacs that branch from a single terminal bronchiole. Parameters: (1) the proximal boundary — the terminal bronchiole at its origin, approximately the 16th generation from the trachea, defining the acinus as its downstream offspring; (2) the internal hierarchy — the respiratory bronchiole (transitional conducting-to-gas-exchange airway with scattered alveolar outpouchings), the alveolar ducts (thin-walled conduits studded with alveoli), and the alveolar sacs (terminal clusters of alveoli sharing a common opening), forming a distal-to-proximal sequence; (3) the gas-exchange architecture — the progressive increase in alveolar surface area distally, so that the alveolar sacs provide the majority of the acinus surface area; (4) the vascular relationship — a dense capillary network adjacent to alveolar walls, forming the alveolar-capillary membrane where gas exchange occurs. It persists as a maintained anatomical landmark in pulmonary histology, respiratory physiology, and emphysema pathology. e.g.: the pulmonary acinus as described in Junqueira Basic Histology, 15th edition; acinar emphysema (centriacinar pattern) in COPD per GOLD criteria; acinar ventilation imaging in West Respiratory Physiology, 10th edition | not: the botanical acinus (a plant morphology term, unrelated); the pulmonary lobule (a larger unit containing multiple acini) [formal: acinus pulmonis | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.name: segmental-bronchus
payload.scope: People made the segmental-bronchus construct to map each named airway branch arising from a lobar bronchus that supplies a single bronchopulmonary segment, so that thoracic surgeons can resect individual segments and bronchoscopists can target localized airway disease.

definition.body: The segmental bronchus is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps each named airway branch arising from a lobar bronchus that supplies a single bronchopulmonary segment. Parameters: (1) the hierarchy — each lobar bronchus divides into named segmental bronchi (typically 3 on the right upper lobe — apical, posterior, anterior; 2 on the right middle lobe — medial and lateral; 3 on the right lower lobe — superior, medial basal, anterior basal, lateral basal, posterior basal; 2 on the left upper lobe — apicoposterior and anterior; 2 on the left lower lobe — superior, inferior), corresponding to the functional segmentation of each pulmonary lobe; (2) the cartilaginous support — hyaline cartilage plates persist in the wall at this level, though fewer than in the lobar generation, maintaining airway patency through the branching point; (3) the vascular companion, each segmental bronchus is accompanied by a branch of the pulmonary artery and surrounded by a lymphatic plexus and autonomic nerves, forming the bronchopulmonary segment as a unit; (4) the clinical target — segmental bronchi are directly visualizable by rigid or flexible bronchoscopy and serve as landmarks for segmental resection, biopsy targeting, and bronchoscopic lung volume reduction. It persists as a maintained organizational framework in thoracic surgery, pulmonology, and radiological anatomy. e.g.: the segmental bronchus classification in Gray's Anatomy 42nd edition; right upper lobe anterior segmental bronchus targeted for endobronchial valve placement in emphysema treatment; segmental bronchus identification during video-assisted thoracoscopic segmentectomy | not: the lobar bronchus (the larger parent airway from which segmental bronchi branch); the subsegmental-bronchus (the smaller airway branching from the segmental bronchus); the bronchopulmonary-segment (the functional unit containing the bronchus, artery, and lymphatics) [formal: bronchus segmentalis | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.name: pulmonary-lobule
payload.scope: People made the pulmonary-lobule construct to map the smallest structural unit of lung tissue — a polygonal cluster of alveoli and their associated airways supplied by a single terminal bronchiole — so that pathologists can localize disease processes and radiologists can correlate imaging findings with anatomical units.

definition.body: The pulmonary lobule is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps the smallest structural and functional unit of the lung, centered on a terminal bronchiole and comprising all lung tissue distal to it within its domain of supply. Parameters: (1) the center, each lobule is organized around a central arteriole (branch of the pulmonary artery) and its accompanying terminal bronchiole, from which the lobule's architecture radiates outward; (2) the boundaries — the lobule is delimited by connective tissue septa that extend from the visceral pleura, separating it from adjacent lobules; these septa contain the draining lymphatics and pulmonary veins; (3) the internal structure, within each lobule the terminal bronchiole gives rise to respiratory bronchioles, each of which branches into alveolar ducts that lead to clusters of alveoli and alveolar sacs — the gas-exchange parenchyma; (4) the size — a pulmonary lobule is approximately 1 to 2.5 centimeters in diameter, visible to the naked eye as a polygonal unit on the pleural surface; (5) the clinical relevance, the lobule is the unit of organization for many disease processes — centrilobular emphysema, centrilobular nodules on high-resolution CT, and bronchiolitis all pattern themselves to this structural unit. It persists as a maintained organizational unit in radiological anatomy, pathology, and pulmonary medicine. e.g.: High-Resolution CT of the Lung by Hansbo and Hatabu 3rd edition; centrilobular emphysema pattern on HRCT per Fleischner Society glossary; pulmonary lobule anatomy in Gray's Anatomy 42nd edition | not: the acinus (smaller gas-exchange unit within a lobule); the bronchopulmonary-segment (larger surgical unit containing many lobules) [formal: lobulus pulmonis | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.name: main-bronchus
payload.scope: People made the main-bronchus construct to map each of the two principal airways emerging from the tracheal bifurcation, so that surgeons and radiologists can identify the proximal landmark for lobar-bronchus isolation and bronchopulmonary segment targeting.

definition.body: The main bronchus is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps each of the two primary airways arising from the tracheal bifurcation at the carina, supplying the right and left lungs. Parameters: (1) the bifurcation landmark — the point at the sternal angle (approximately T4–T5 vertebral level) where the trachea divides into the right and left main bronchi; (2) the right-left asymmetry — the right main bronchus is shorter, wider, and more vertical than the left, reflecting the anterior position of the heart and the lateral extent of the right lung; (3) the length and course — the right main bronchus measures approximately 2.5 cm and gives rise to the eparterial bronchus before entering the right lung; the left main bronchus measures approximately 5 cm and courses laterally beneath the aortic arch to enter the left lung; (4) the wall structure — supported by C-shaped hyaline cartilage plates continuous with the tracheal rings, with the posterior membranous wall facing the esophagus. It persists as a maintained anatomical landmark in thoracic surgery, bronchoscopy, radiographic interpretation, and respiratory anatomy. e.g.: the right main bronchus as the target of bronchoscope insertion beyond the carina; the left main bronchus seen on axial chest CT at the level of the aortic arch; surgical clamping of the right main bronchus during right pneumonectomy | not: the trachea (the single airway proximal to the bifurcation); the lobar bronchus (the distal branch arising from the main bronchus) [formal: bronchus principalis | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.name: terminal-bronchiole
payload.scope: People made the terminal-bronchiole construct to map the last conducting airway generation before gas exchange begins, so that pathologists and physiologists can define the boundary between the conducting and respiratory zones of the lung.

definition.body: The terminal bronchiole is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps the final generation of conducting airways, distal to the subsegmental bronchus and proximal to the respiratory bronchiole, where the transition from conduction to gas exchange begins. Parameters: (1) the generational position — approximately the 22nd to 23rd generation from the trachea, branching from the subsegmental bronchus and giving rise to the respiratory bronchiole; (2) the cartilage boundary — the last airway generation entirely free of hyaline cartilage in its wall, distinguishing it from the cartilage-bearing bronchi proximal; (3) the epithelial transition — lined by simple cuboidal epithelium with Clara (club) cells, a change from the ciliated pseudostratified columnar epithelium of proximal bronchioles; (4) the smooth muscle prominence — relatively thick smooth muscle layers that confer significant bronchoconstrictive capability despite the small internal diameter (0.5 to 1.0 mm). It persists as a maintained landmark in pulmonary histology, respiratory physiology, occupational lung disease classification, and bronchiolar pathology. e.g.: the terminal bronchiole as the histological reference for respiratory zone demarcation in lung biopsy reports; terminal bronchiolar metaplasia documented in smokers' lung tissue sections; terminal bronchiole caliber measured by high-resolution CT in bronchiolitis obliterans syndrome | not: the respiratory bronchiole (the airway where gas exchange first occurs, branching from the terminal bronchiole); the subsegmental bronchus (the cartilage-bearing airway proximal to the terminal bronchiole) [formal: bronchiolus terminalis | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.name: airway
payload.scope: People made the airway construct to map the passages conducting air from the external environment to the gas-exchange surfaces of the lung parenchyma, so that clinicians and physiologists can categorize airway diseases by anatomical level and plan airway management interventions.

definition.body: The airway is a human-authored anatomical category that maps the passages conducting and conditioning air from the external environment to the gas-exchange surfaces of the lung. Parameters: (1) the functional role — conducting inspired air and conditioning it (warming, humidifying, filtering particulates) before it reaches the alveoli; (2) the anatomical extent — from the nares through the upper respiratory tract (nasal cavity, pharynx, larynx) to the lower respiratory tract (trachea, bronchi, bronchioles) and finally to the respiratory bronchioles where gas exchange begins; (3) the structural gradient — cartilage support from complete C-shaped rings in the trachea, to irregular plates in the bronchi, to absent in the bronchioles; (4) the epithelial gradient — pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium (nasal cavity, trachea) through simple cuboidal (bronchioles) to simple squamous (alveolar surface). It persists as a maintained category in respiratory physiology, pulmonary medicine, and clinical airway management. e.g.: the airway classification in West Respiratory Physiology 10th edition; upper airway obstruction in obstructive sleep apnea syndrome per AASM guidelines; bronchoprovocation testing measuring lower airway response to methacholine | not: the alimentary tract (conducts food and liquid, not air, through a separate passage); the respiratory system as a whole (includes vascular and gas-exchange components beyond the conducting airway) [formal: via respiratoria | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.name: spirometry
payload.scope: People made the spirometry construct to map the measurement of lung volumes and flows during breathing, so that clinicians can diagnose obstructive and restrictive lung disease, monitor disease progression, and assess treatment response.

definition.body: The spirometry is a human-authored measurement construct that quantifies lung volumes and flow rates during breathing maneuvers. Parameters: (1) the measured variables — forced vital capacity (FVC), forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1), peak expiratory flow (PEF), and flow-volume loops recorded during the forced breathing maneuver; (2) the standard maneuvers — the maximal inhalation to total lung capacity followed by the maximal forced exhalation until residual volume, held for at least six seconds with acceptable reproducibility (two FEV1 values within 150 mL); (3) the reference equations — predicted values derived from population norms indexed to height, age, sex, and ethnicity (e.g., NHANES III, GLI-2012 reference values); (4) the interpretation thresholds — obstructive patterns defined as FEV1/FVC below the lower limit of normal (LLN), restrictive patterns as reduced FVC with preserved or elevated FEV1/FVC ratio. It persists as the most widely used pulmonary function test, codified in ATS/ERS joint statements and maintained in clinical guidelines worldwide. e.g.: FEV1 measurement per the 2019 ATS/ERS statement on pulmonary function testing; spirometry screening for occupational asthma per American Thoracic Society guidelines; preoperative spirometry assessment for lobectomy candidates in surgical lung-volume reduction trials | not: the spirometer device (the instrument that performs the measurement, not the measurement construct itself); plethysmography (a different method for measuring total lung capacity, using body box principles) [formal: spirometria | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.name: forced-vital-capacity
payload.scope: People made the forced vital capacity construct to map the total volume of air that can be forcibly exhaled after a maximal inhalation, so that clinicians can quantify restrictive ventilatory defects and track disease progression in interstitial lung disease.

definition.body: The forced vital capacity is a human-authored measurement construct that quantifies the maximum volume of air a person can exhale from full lung inflation in a single forced maneuver. Parameters: (1) the maneuver — maximal inhalation to total lung capacity followed by a maximal forced exhalation held for at least six seconds; (2) the measured volume — expressed in liters, indexed to predicted values from NHANES III or GLI-2012 equations adjusted for height, age, sex, and ethnicity; (3) the interpretation — values below 80% of predicted indicate restrictive impairment; 80–100% are within normal limits; (4) the quality criteria — ATS/ERS criteria require acceptable trace, no cough, no early termination, and reproducibility between maneuvers within 150 mL. It persists as a maintained spirometric parameter, codified in ATS/ERS joint statements and used globally in pulmonary function laboratories. e.g.: FVC measurement per the 2019 ATS/ERS pulmonary function statement; FVC tracking in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis per ATS/ERS ILD guideline; GLI-2012 spirometry reference values in the European Respiratory Journal | not: the total lung capacity (includes residual volume, not exhalable); the FEV1 (volume exhaled in the first second of the FVC maneuver) [formal: capacitas vitalis forzata | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.name: peak-expiratory-flow
payload.scope: People made the peak expiratory flow construct to map the maximum speed of exhalation from full lung inflation, so that clinicians can quickly screen for obstructive airway disease and monitor asthma severity at the bedside.

definition.body: The peak expiratory flow is a human-authored measurement construct that quantifies the maximum flow rate achieved during a forced exhalation from full lung inflation. Parameters: (1) the maneuver — maximal inhalation to total lung capacity followed by the fastest possible forced exhalation, with the peak occurring in the first tenth to one-fifth of the exhalation; (2) the measured variable — peak flow expressed in liters per minute, typically measured with a peak flow meter; (3) the reference values — predicted norms derived from population equations indexed to height, age, sex, and ethnicity; (4) the clinical thresholds — values below 50% of predicted indicate severe obstruction; 50–80% moderate; above 80% mild or normal. It persists as the most widely used bedside pulmonary function measurement, codified in GINA asthma guidelines and used in occupational health screening. e.g.: peak flow monitoring per the GINA 2024 asthma management guidelines; PEF measurement in workplace asthma surveillance per the American College of Occupational and Environmental Medicine; PEF-based asthma action plans in the British Thoracic Society asthma guideline | not: the peak flow meter device (the instrument that measures PEF, not the parameter itself); the forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1, a different spirometric parameter measuring volume not flow rate) [formal: fluxus exspiratorius peakus | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.name: alveolar-capillary-membrane
payload.scope: People made the alveolar-capillary membrane construct to map the thin diffusion barrier between alveolar air and pulmonary capillary blood, so that physiologists can model gas exchange, pathologists can assess interstitial lung disease, and clinicians can interpret diffusing capacity measurements.

definition.body: The alveolar-capillary membrane is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps the thin diffusion barrier separating alveolar air from pulmonary capillary blood, where oxygen and carbon dioxide cross between the respiratory and circulatory systems. Parameters: (1) the layered architecture — the alveolar epithelium (a continuous sheet of type I pneumocyte cytoplasm), the fused basal laminae of epithelium and endothelium forming a single shared basement membrane, and the capillary endothelium; (2) the thickness gradient — ranging from 0.2 micrometers at the thinnest gas-exchange sites to 1.0 micrometer in thicker regions, optimized for diffusion efficiency; (3) the surfactant lining — a monomolecular layer of pulmonary surfactant on the alveolar surface that modifies the effective diffusion distance; (4) the capillary bed — a dense perialveolar capillary network whose blood volume and wall tension influence the effective surface area available for gas exchange. It persists as a maintained anatomical landmark in respiratory physiology, pulmonary histology, and clinical gas-exchange assessment. e.g.: the alveolar-capillary membrane as described in West Respiratory Physiology 10th edition; electron micrograph of the blood-air barrier in Robbins Basic Pathology 11th edition; diffusing capacity of the lung for carbon monoxide measurement per ATS ERS guidelines | not: the pulmonary capillary (the blood vessel containing blood, not the diffusion barrier itself); the alveolar wall (the broader septal structure including connective tissue, not specifically the gas-exchange membrane) [formal: membrana alveolocapillaris | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.name: upper-airway
payload.scope: People made the upper-airway category to name the proximal segment of the respiratory airway, so that clinicians can localize the site of airway obstruction and anticipate the difficult airway.

definition.body: The upper-airway category is a human-made clinical classification that names the proximal segment of the respiratory airway and draws its distal boundary against the lower airway. Parameters: (1) the disputed distal boundary, the category's defining work is where it ends: otolaryngology's classic airway classification ends it at the vocal folds (the glottic plane), the anesthesiology and airway-management literature often ends it at the lower border of the cricoid cartilage, and some surgical atlases cut it at the thoracic inlet, so the category is the airway lying above whichever landmark a given map chooses and the same tube is 'upper' to one map and split between 'upper' and 'lower' to another; (2) the proximal extent, the category takes in the nasal cavities and nasopharynx, the oropharynx, and the laryngeal inlet down to the chosen landmark; (3) the maintenance, the category persists in airway classification systems, ENT and anesthesiology teaching, the topographic classification of airway obstruction (supraglottic, glottic, subglottic), and the clinical entity of upper airway obstruction; what holds it is the naming and its use, not the tissue. e.g.: the otolaryngology teaching that the upper airway spans the nares to the vocal folds in standard ENT airway atlases; the anesthesiology airway classification that extends the upper airway to the cricoid in the difficult-airway literature; the upper-airway-obstruction diagnostic category that localizes obstructive sleep apnea to the pharynx or supraglottis | not: the trachea (the named airway straddling the disputed boundary, an organ-level entry, not the segment category); the bronchial tree (the more distal map of the intrapulmonary airways) [formal: via aerea superior | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.name: conducting-zone
payload.scope: People made the conducting-zone partition to set off the gas-exchanging portion of the airways, so that physiologists can quantify dead space and clinicians can localize where obstruction and resistance arise.

definition.body: The conducting zone is a human-made physiological partition that groups the airways that convey air without gas exchange, from the trachea down to the terminal bronchiole. Parameters: (1) membership, the zone takes in the trachea, the main, lobar and segmental bronchi, and the bronchioles, and ends at the terminal bronchiole, the last purely conducting airway; (2) the boundary, its distal limit is the first respiratory bronchiole, where the wall first opens onto alveoli and gas exchange begins, and that line is drawn by the appearance of the first alveolar opening, not by the loss of cartilage or by caliber, so it separates the conducting zone from the respiratory zone at a single airway generation; (3) the defining property, every airway in the zone conducts air but performs no gas exchange, which is why the volume of the zone is the anatomical dead space that enters the lung's gas-exchange equations; (4) maintenance, the zone persists in respiratory physiology and pulmonary-function testing, where the conducting-versus-respiratory division grounds the measurement of dead space and the flow-volume curve. e.g.: the trachea and its bronchial branches as the proximal conducting airways in a respiratory-physiology text; the terminal bronchiole as the last purely conducting airway in a pulmonary-physiology text; the anatomical dead-space volume computed as the volume of the conducting airways in spirometry | not: the respiratory zone (the gas-exchanging airways distal to the terminal bronchiole, the complementary partition); the bronchial tree (the structural map of the branching airways, which spans both zones) [formal: zona conductiva | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.name: respiratory-zone
payload.scope: People made the respiratory-zone partition to set off the gas-exchanging portion of the airways, so that physiologists can locate where oxygen and carbon dioxide cross and model the gas-exchange surface.

definition.body: The respiratory zone is a human-made physiological partition that groups the airways in which gas exchange occurs, from the first respiratory bronchiole down to the alveoli. Parameters: (1) membership, the zone takes in the respiratory bronchioles, the alveolar ducts and the alveolar sacs, beginning at the first respiratory bronchiole, the first airway whose wall opens onto alveoli; (2) the boundary, its proximal limit is the terminal bronchiole, the last purely conducting airway, so the zone starts at the airway generation where the first alveolar opening appears, and that line is drawn by the appearance of gas-exchange surface, not by the loss of cartilage or by caliber, which separates the respiratory zone from the conducting zone at a single airway generation; (3) the defining property, every airway in the zone participates in gas exchange, so its walls carry the alveolar surface and the capillary network, and the zone is where the lung performs its gas-exchange function; (4) maintenance, the zone persists in respiratory physiology and pulmonary pathology, where the conducting-versus-respiratory division grounds the location of gas-exchange disease and the measurement of the respiratory surface. e.g.: the respiratory bronchiole as the first gas-exchanging airway in a respiratory-physiology text; the alveolar ducts and sacs as the gas-exchanging airways in a pulmonary-histology text; the gas-exchange surface of the zone as the site of diffusion in a respiratory-physiology text | not: the conducting zone (conveying air without gas exchange, the complementary partition); the bronchial tree (the structural map spanning both zones) [formal: zona respiratoria | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

definition.body: The lower-airway category is a human-made clinical classification that names the distal segment of the respiratory airway and draws its proximal boundary against the upper airway. Parameters: (1) the disputed proximal boundary, the category's defining work is where it begins: anesthesiology and airway-management literature often start it below the lower border of the cricoid cartilage, surgical atlases start it at the thoracic inlet, and some classifications start it at the glottic plane, so the category is the airway lying below whichever landmark a given map chooses and the same trachea is 'lower' to one map and split between 'upper' and 'lower' to another; (2) the distal extent, the category takes in the trachea below the chosen landmark, the main, lobar and segmental bronchi, the bronchioles, and the gas-exchanging airways down to the alveoli; (3) the maintenance, the category persists in clinical airway classification, the topographic division of airway obstruction, the radiology and bronchoscopy literature, and the clinical entity of lower-airway disease; what holds it is the naming and its use, not the tissue. e.g.: the trachea below the cricoid as the proximal lower airway in an anesthesiology airway classification; the intrathoracic trachea and bronchi as the lower airways in a radiology atlas; the lower-airway disease category that groups asthma and bronchiolitis in a pulmonology text | not: the upper airway (the proximal segment, the complementary category with the same disputed line); the bronchial tree (the structural map of the intrapulmonary airways) [formal: via aerea inferior | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.name: small-airway
payload.scope: People made the small-airways category to name the distal airways below the cartilage-bearing bronchi, so that clinicians can detect early obstructive disease before it reaches the large airways.

definition.body: The small-airways category is a human-made clinical and physiological classification that names the distal airways, the bronchioles, below the last cartilage-bearing airways. Parameters: (1) the boundary, the category's defining line is the loss of cartilage: it begins at the first airway without cartilage plates, the terminal bronchiole generation, and the airways it names are the bronchioles and their branches down to the respiratory bronchioles, so the line is drawn by the structure of the wall, the last cartilage plate, not by a single named landmark; (2) the flow property, below this caliber the airflow is laminar rather than turbulent and the airways offer little measurable resistance, which is why early obstruction hides here until the late, detectable phase; (3) the clinical unit, the category persists as the site of small-airways disease, the earliest obstructive lesion in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and as the target of the slow vital capacity and the closing-volume test that probe it; (4) maintenance, the category persists in the pulmonology and respiratory-physiology literature, the histology of the bronchiole, and the clinical staging of airway disease. e.g.: the bronchioles as the cartilage-free airways named by the small-airways category in a respiratory-physiology text; the small-airways disease entity in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease in a pulmonology text; the closing-volume and slow-vital-capacity tests that probe the small airways in a pulmonary-function text | not: the bronchus (the cartilage-bearing airways, proximal to the boundary); the conducting zone (the functional partition defined by gas exchange, not by caliber or cartilage) [formal: viae aereae minores | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.name: airway
payload.scope: People made the airway category to name the whole air passage as a single functional unit, so that clinicians can manage, clear, and protect it across the organs that line it.

definition.body: The airway category is a human-made functional classification that names the entire passage air takes from the outside world to the alveoli and back. Parameters: (1) the span, the category takes in every air-bearing space along the passage, the upper airway (the nasal cavities, the nasopharynx and oropharynx, the laryngeal inlet), the trachea, and the lower airway (the bronchi, the bronchioles, and the alveoli), so the upper and lower airways are its named segments and the category is their functional whole; (2) the boundary, its limits are drawn by the continuity of the air passage, not by organ: it begins where inspired air enters the body, at the nares and mouth, and ends where air reaches the gas-exchange surface, at the alveoli, so the airway is the passage rather than any one of the structures that line it, and the larynx, which it takes in whole, is in while the esophagus, which shares the pharynx, is out for not carrying the air passage; (3) the clinical unit, the category persists as the object of airway management and the site of airway obstruction, and as the axis on which the upper-versus-lower division is drawn; (4) maintenance, what holds it is the naming and its clinical use in anesthesiology, otolaryngology, and emergency medicine. e.g.: the airway as the functional whole from the nares to the alveoli in a standard anatomy text; the upper-and-lower airway division of the airway in a clinical airway-management text; the airway as the site of obstruction in the difficult-airway classification in an anesthesiology text | not: the bronchial tree (the intrapulmonary branching map, not the whole passage); the esophagus (the food passage sharing the pharynx, excluded by the air it does not carry) [formal: via aerea | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]
